paragraphs.text: Lesson 26, a great vacation.
Kate has just returned from vacation, and Julia asks her about it.
Listen to their conversation and answer the comprehension questions.
Hey Kate, welcome back. How was your vacation?
It was wonderful. Norway's an amazing place.
I saw some breathtaking scenery and I feel like I got to recharge my batteries.
How is the weather?
There's a Norwegian expression.
We don't have summer, just two months of crummy ski conditions.
So even though it was June, it was chilly.
We were all bundled up in fleeces and winter hats.
And meanwhile here we've been having a heatwave.
What was the country like?
Oh, the spectacular countryside more than made up for the cool weather.
Norway has the rolling hills of Ireland and the snow-capped mountains of the Canadian Rockies.
We explored these little water inlets where you could spot at least one waterfall from anywhere you stood.
That sounds incredible. How did it stack up against all the other places you've been?
Well, it was the most expensive city in Europe I've been to, so that's one downside.
We splurged on a nice hotel, so we didn't have much left over for food.
Basically we ate brown bread and cheese the entire time.
But I definitely go back, especially if I had a friend in the city that I could crash with.
You're lucky you can just take off and travel whenever the impulse strikes.
I wish I could travel more, but my boss doesn't let me take much time off.
She says I'm indispensable.
I'm not sure if that's a blessing or a curse.
But you do have your honeymoon next year, right? Remind me where you're going again?
Um, our plans are still up in the air.
Actually, I'd love to hear your take. Of all the places you've been, which one do you recommend the most?
That's a really tough question. It all hinges on what you're looking for.
If you want classy architecture in a romantic city, definitely go to Paris.
It's well-preserved because France was quick to surrender during World War II,
so it's like you're visiting a different time period.
A lot of other cities still have old buildings, of course, but they're mixed in with modern skyscrapers as well.
Good to know. Do you have any other pointers?
If you want a more traditional honeymoon atmosphere in a warm climate, try the Greek islands.
All the villages are built into the rocky cliff face, and the houses are white,
which is a striking contrast to the sparkling blue ocean.
For delicious food, a rich history, and friendly, outgoing people, check out Italy.
And if you're looking for a quaint, bed-and-breakfast type place in the countryside, I'd recommend Ireland.
I've got to jot this down. All these places sound great. It seems impossible to choose just one.
Why not quit your job? Then you'd have all the time in the world to travel.
Sure, but then I couldn't afford to go anywhere.
Alright, let's learn the vocabulary from Kate and Julia's conversation.
Kate saw some breathtaking scenery.
Breath-taking scenery means views that are amazingly beautiful.
And she feels like she got to recharge her batteries.
This is an expression that means relax and recover your energy.
Kate cites a Norwegian expression that they don't have summer, just two months of crummy ski conditions.
The word crummy is an informal word for bad.
So even though it was June, it was chilly in Norway.
Chilly means rather cold.
Kate and her travel partner were all bundled up in fleeces and winter hats.
Bundled up means dressed in warm clothing. And fleeces are a type of jacket.
You can click the link in the text lesson for a picture.
Meanwhile, where Julia's living, they've been having a heat wave.
A heat wave is a sequence of many very hot days in a row.
Kate says that the spectacular countryside more than made up for the cool weather.
More than made up for means it definitely compensated for.
In other words, the spectacular countryside was much better than the cool weather was bad.
Norway has some snow-capped mountains.
Snow-capped means there is snow on top of the mountains.
And Kate explored a place where you could spot at least one waterfall from anywhere you stood.
The verb spot is an informal word for sea.
Julia asks Kate how Norway stacked up against the other places she's been.
To stack up against means compare to.
And Kate talks about one of the downsides.
A downside is a disadvantage, the fact that it was expensive.
Kate splurged on a nice hotel.
Displayed on something means to spend an extra amount of money on something that's luxurious.
Not a necessity.
Kate says she'd definitely go back though, especially if she had a friend in the city that she could crash with.
The phrasal verb crash with means to stay at someone's house.
It's an informal way to say this.
Julia thinks Kate is lucky she can just take off and travel whenever the impulse strikes.
Whenever the impulse strikes means whenever you want to, spontaneously.
Julia can't take much time off because her boss says she's indispensable at work.
Indispensable means essential. It's impossible to be without Julia at work.
Julia is not sure if that's a blessing, a good thing, or a curse, a terrible thing.
But she does have her honeymoon next year.
A honeymoon is a trip or a vacation taken by married couples after their wedding.
Julia's plans for her honeymoon are still up in the air.
If your plans are up in the air, it means they are not yet finalized, not yet confirmed.
And Julia says to Kate, I'd love to hear your take.
Your take means your opinion.
Kate says the best place to travel hinges on what you're looking for.
Hinges on is another way to say depends on.
Kate recommends Paris for its classy architecture.
The adjective classy means elegant or refined.
Other cities also have old buildings, but they're usually mixed in with modern skyscrapers as well.
Skyscrapers are very tall buildings, usually modern ones.
Julia asks Kate if she has any other pointers.
Pointers is another word for tips.
For a warm destination, Kate suggests the Greek islands, with villages that are built into the rocky cliff face.
Villages are small communities, and a cliff is a steep, vertical rock wall.
The houses on the Greek islands are white, which is a striking contrast to the sparkling blue ocean.
If something is striking, it means it grabs your attention and produces a strong impression on your sight or mind.
And the sparkling blue ocean.
If something is sparkling, it means it has little bits of light.
Kate recommends going to Italy for delicious food, a rich history, and friendly, outgoing people.
If a person is outgoing, it means he or she is extroverted and really enjoys socializing.
And Kate says, if you're looking for a quaint, bed and breakfast type place in the countryside, she'd recommend Ireland.
The word quaint means old-fashioned and charming.
Julia replies, I've got to jot this down.
Jot this down is an informal way to say, write this down.
Julia thinks all the places sound so great, it seems impossible to choose.
Kate comments, why not quit your job, then you'd have all the time in the world to travel.
The expression all the time in the world means a lot of time, or infinite time, without a particular deadline to finish.
Julia says, sure, but then I couldn't afford to go anywhere, so if she quit her job, she'd have time, but no money to travel.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
